method: Earnings of each country's companies (owner or manager of the ship, insurer, lender, registry; never the flag of convenience as owner) from Russian seaborne crude, oil-product and LNG exports. EUR bn at ECB yearly averages; 2026 = Jan-Aug. (1) Freight: a yearly gross freight pool in USD (crude: barrels x average freight per barrel across long-haul Baltic/Black Sea-India/China and short-haul Kozmino/Europe routes; products: barrels x product-tanker freight; LNG: Arc7 and conventional carrier charter earnings) = crude 3.0/3.6/2.2, products 2.5/2.4/2.0, LNG 0.8/0.9/1.0 for 2019/2020/2021; 2022 8.5/5.0/1.3; 2023 11.0/5.0/1.2; 2024 8.1/4.0/1.1; 2025 7.2/3.6/1.1; 2026 Jan-Aug 9.7/3.6/0.8. Freight per barrel follows Reuters/Argus voyage quotes (Baltic-India Aframax ~USD 20m record 2022, 7.8m Apr 2023, Suezmax 27-30m Oct 2023, 4.7-8m in 2025, 16-23m Mar-Apr 2026) and volumes from KSE/CREA (seaborne crude ~3.3-3.5 mb/d, products ~2.1-2.4 mb/d, LNG ~30-33 Mt). The pool is split by owner/manager country with yearly shares from CREA, S&P Global, Windward, Global Witness and FT evidence; Russian-owned and Russian-controlled tankers (Sovcomflot and fronts registered in the UAE/HK etc., about 45% of UAE-registered shadow tonnage) form a Russian pool that is not assigned to any foreign country. Opaque owners (2-5.5%) are spread over the shadow hubs (UAE 35%, HK 20%, China 15%, India 15%, Vietnam/Seychelles/Malaysia 5% each) so missing ownership data never counts as zero. Gross freight is revenue, not profit: time-charter-equivalent earnings are ~60-75% of it, the rest is bunkers and port costs. (2) Ship sales: second-hand tankers sold to shadow-fleet buyers by seller country (FTM: >230 Western tankers, >USD 6bn; Greece ~USD 4bn, UK 0.59, Germany 0.19, Belgium 0.135; non-Western sellers educated guesses), timed 38/37/17/6/2% over 2022-2026. Counted value = 40% of sale price (the price premium over scrap/pre-war values for 15-20-year-old tonnage), low 20% x 0.7, high 80% x 1.5 (the full sale value when the buyer is clearly Russia-linked). No baseline (there was no shadow-fleet demand before 2022). (3) Insurance/finance/management: P&I+hull premiums = tanker-equivalents in Russian trade (340-350 pre-war, 550 in 2022, ~700 from 2023) x USD 0.45-0.6m per ship-year, split by insurer country (IG clubs in the UK, Norway, Sweden, Luxembourg, US, Japan before the Dec 2022 ban; Ingosstrakh and other Russian insurers, plus Indian, UAE and Chinese providers after); cargo insurance (0.04% of export value), third-party management fees (USD 0.18m per ship-year) and a finance margin (2-5% of freight) follow the owner shares. (4) Registry fees: ship-years x USD 20-35k by flag share; Liberian and Marshall Islands fees split 50/50 with their US-based operators. (5) Baseline 2019-2021 = mean of the three years for freight, insurance/finance and registry. Ranges ~90%: country range = common pool uncertainty (x0.65-x1.45) combined with share uncertainty by certainty (B x0.7-1.35, C x0.5-1.8, D x0.35/0.4-2.2/2.5) as independent log errors. Totals keep the pool error fully correlated. Produced by the project's research step and kept as a data input; the research scripts are not in the repository, and the sources are listed in the notes.

overlap: Mostly NOT inside uncovered.json services, with a small overlap. In balance-of-payments terms freight on an export is a transaction between the carrier and whoever charters the ship. Russian oil is mostly sold to non-resident buyers (Indian and Chinese refiners) or offshore traders in Dubai and Hong Kong. Those buyers and traders pay the freight, so the money does not pass through Russia's balance of payments. It therefore does not appear in the carriers' services exports to Russia, which is what Eurostat/BaTiS sold_to_rus measures. Evidence: (a) Russia's total sea-freight imports from all countries fell from USD 4.6bn (2021) to 3.7 (2022), 3.6 (2023) and 2.8 (2024, 2025) (Bank of Russia). Over the same years the foreign-owned freight on Russian oil in this file rose to USD 10-14bn, so at most a small part can sit in Russia's imports. Most of Russia's sea-freight imports pay for its own imports (containers, CIF). (b) BaTiS transport exports to Russia for Greece rose only from USD 0.18bn (2021) to 0.29/0.33/0.39bn (2022-24). That is 4-8% of the Greek earnings estimated here; Cyprus, Malta, Norway and Denmark fell. (c) Russia's insurance imports collapsed from USD 1.2bn (2021) to 0.4 (2022) and below 0.15 (2023-25). So most P&I on Russian-trade tankers is paid by non-Russian owners and is not in sold_to_rus. Share to remove to avoid double counting with sold_to_rus: freight 5% (0-15%); insurance/finance 20% (5-40%) for 2021-2022, when Sovcomflot and Russian charterers still bought Western P&I and services, and 10% (0-25%) from 2023; ship sales 0% (they are goods, not services; direct sales to Russian-resident buyers could sit in goods trade, HS 8901, high 10%); registry 0%. The 2021 values in this file carry the same shares, so the baseline is treated alike. Overlap with the Greek item uncovered.json GRC.oil_shipping_earned: this file replaces it (it covered Greek crude freight only). Do not add both. Overlap with crea.json fossil payments: crude is valued free-on-board at Russian ports (CREA methodology), so crude freight is not inside buyers' payments to Russia (0%). Products and LNG are priced with Eurostat import unit values, which are CIF, so an amount close to EU-route freight (USD 2-5/bbl) is probably embedded in the payments credited to Russia. That is roughly 30-60% of the products and LNG freight here, or about 10-20% of total freight. It is a valuation issue in the fossil figures: the money goes to the carriers, not to Russia. The cleaner fix is to trim CREA product values. Russian-owned and Russian-controlled tankers (totals.russia_own_and_controlled, EUR 2.5-3.4bn a year) are not a foreign country's earnings and are not assigned.
